 As Ted Schuur stepped along the edges of Smith Lake, a bubble surfaced from the muck underfoot. And then another.
They're bubbles of methane, a potent heat-trapping gas made from decomposing plants and animals that had once been stuck in Alaska's frigid permafrost. But that frozen ground is thawing because the Arctic is warming four times faster than the rest of the globe. For thousands of years that frozen ground stored dead plants and animals, but the accelerating thaw is allowing them to decay into methane and carbon dioxide. 
“Once you start leaking this carbon out, there’s so much in the ground that it’s not going to shut off,” said Schuur, an ecologist at Northern Arizona University, calling it one of climate change's scary tipping points. “Essentially every year is setting a permafrost record.”





There’s three times as much carbon still frozen in permafrost than what’s now in the air, but all over the Arctic those heat-trapping gases are escaping into the atmosphere. Their release adds to what's already in the air from humanity's burning coal, oil and natural gas, changing the delicate balance of how a warming world deals with the buildup of heat-trapping carbon, Schuur said.
Permafrost is ground that stays frozen — below 32 degrees Fahrenheit (zero degrees Celsius) — for at least two years and often for centuries and even millennia. That frozen ground — found in Alaska, Canada, Siberia, Antarctica and high mountain elevations elsewhere — has special advantages, trapping decaying matter, keeping it from turning into greenhouse gases and just being firm enough for communities and industries to build their lives upon.

 A wind turbine described by its developer as the world’s tallest now rises 365 meters (1,197 feet) above the sparsely populated landscape of eastern Germany, surpassing the height of the Eiffel Tower.
The colossal turbine has been built at an existing wind farm in Lusatia, southeast of Berlin. Once a major center of lignite mining, the region has increasingly turned to renewable energy in recent years. The prototype reached its full height this week and is due to be inaugurated in mid-November.
Jochen Grossmann, chief executive of Gircon, the Dresden-based engineering company that built the tower, said the structure would harness the stronger, more reliable winds found at greater heights. Conventional wind turbines typically have a hub height — the distance from the ground to the center of the rotor — of well below 200 meters (656 feet).





“At 300 meters, we have such constant and strong wind that we can produce more than twice as much electrical energy as with the same facility at today's heights,” Grossmann said on Thursday. He added that it would also be possible to produce electricity for much more of the year than with existing turbines.
The turbine has a hub height of 300 meters (984 feet), and its rotor blades bring its total height to 365 meters. That makes it taller than the Eiffel Tower in Paris, at 330 meters (1,083 feet), and leaves it just short of Berlin's television tower, Germany 's tallest building at 368 meters (1,207 feet).

US datacenter discharged large amounts of pollution for almost a year with no permits


Records show Vineland facility in New Jersey emitted health-harming pollution before regulators stepped in




DataOne, the Microsoft-linked New Jersey datacenter recently hit with a $1m fine for running unpermitted generators, emitted large amounts of health-harming air pollution for nearly a year before state regulators stepped in, according to public records obtained by Floodlight.
The Vineland facility’s 62 gas-fired generators became public in August after a Floodlight/Guardian visual investigation found them operating without permits. The New Jersey department of environmental protection last week fined the company over the fleet but did not disclose how long the generators had been operating nor how much air pollution they had released into the surrounding community over the past year.

Floodlight sent technical data about the generators – obtained through public records requests – to a Rutgers professor and a former EPA air division chief.
“Our best estimate is that the generators emitted about 140 tons of NOx,” said Xiaomeng Jin, an assistant professor at Rutgers department of environmental sciences. Her analysis would rank DataOne in the state’s top five NOx polluters of 2025, per EPA data.
NOx are a dangerous group of smog-producing gases linked to asthma, heart attacks and even premature death. It’s “the most important air pollutant in the US that affects most people”, Jin said.
Longtime Vineland resident Tiffany Leone-Vespa lives about a mile from the data center and said the noise from the generators sounds like an airplane in the back of her house.
“What health problems might I face in the future? Because I’ve been exposed to all of that. My kids have been exposed to it,” she said.
The site’s potential NOx emissions are even larger, according to Jin and Bruce Buckheit – a former EPA air enforcement division chief. Both concluded that at full use, DataOne’s fleet could emit more than 1,500 tons of NOx per year. That is nearly twice the amount that the Linden Cogeneration gas-fired power plant, New Jersey’s largest NOx emitter, is allowed to emit.
Operating the generators “results in very high levels of air pollution” and the fleet’s potential emissions are “well over the regulatory threshold for a new major source”, said Buckheit.
New Jersey labels any facility capable of emitting more than 25 tons of NOx per year a “major source”. Obtaining a major source permit requires extensive environmental reviews, best available pollution controls and public comment periods – all before construction can even begin.

Gavin Newsom says Trump is a ‘gift’ to the climate cause for dispelling notions of fossil fuel energy security




Of all the epithets hurled at Donald Trump since he became US president, perhaps the most unusual was delivered last week – that he is, in fact, some sort of environmentalist.
Trump is the “greatest gift” to the environmental movement, argued Gavin Newsom, California’s governor, due to the fallout from the US-Israel war on Iran.

“He’s woken the world up to how vulnerable we are to petro-dictatorships, how vulnerable we are to disruptions in the Middle East,” Newsom told the Guardian during Climate Week in New York. “This war has completely gutted any sort of romantic notions of energy security and it’s compelled folks to think differently. It’s accelerating investments and clean energy and renewables.”


If Trump has been an accidental environmentalist, it’s been in the international sphere. The strait of Hormuz, where a fifth of the world’s oil and gas exports usually flow, is now starting to open up but has been routinely snarled since the Iran war began in February, causing the cost of these fossil fuels to soar around the world.
Countries reacted by scrambling to cut their oil and gas use while turning to cleaner forms of energy such as solar and wind (although there’s also been a small uptick in coal, the dirtiest of fossil fuels).
The overall consequence has been a positive one for our shared climate, with global fossil fuel emissions set to drop by 0.5% this year due to the crisis, Carbon Brief has estimated. The peak in oil consumption may have been sped up enough to arrive this year, rather than the previous estimate of 2029, according to the International Energy Agency.



By launching the war, Trump is set to achieve something only dreamed about by climate advocates and not seen outside global economic crashes or the Covid-19 pandemic – an annual reduction in the emissions that are overheating our planet. The last “super” El Niño to hit London a decade ago brought devastating storms and freezing weather, with experts fearing this winter’s will bring even worse.




The “Godzilla” El Niño expected to hit London this winter could be one of the worst on record, according to experts.








Storm Desmond killed three people and destroyed over 5,000 homes during the winter of 2015/16, the last time there was an El Niño of similar magnitude affecting the UK.




However, the Met Office has said that the El Niño event developing in the tropical Pacific has already “surpassed the magnitude of previous events including the one in 2015/16”.




The national forecaster is predicting a stormier start than usual to autumn and winter, and colder spells at the end of winter.


How have previous ‘El Niño’ events impacted London?




London has been battered by El Niños in a number of previous winters, most significantly in 2015 and 2016.











The event brought Storm Desmond to the UK in early December, with severe gales and record-breaking rainfall hitting much of the country.


Rescue teams evacuate people from their homes after Storm Desmond caused flooding in Carlisle
Jeff J Mitchell/Getty Images

‘The toll is huge’: El Niño-driven wildfires overwhelm Indonesia’s orangutan population


The global climate phenomenon has triggered devastating infernos in the ape’s Indonesian heartlands, with long-term effects on the animals still unknown




The mother’s hands were peeling from walking on the torched ground. Her eight-month-old baby, which clung to her side, was dehydrated and thin. The pair, named Mama Abu and Abu (“ash” in Indonesian), were found in an oil palm subsidiary estate, rescuers say.
The orangutan pair were saved last month from wildfires that are devouring Indonesia’s forests and peatland, unleashing thick smog, and destroying the habitat of some of the planet’s most vulnerable species.

Primate specialists from the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) have called for urgent international assistance to help control the fires, warning this week that thousands of orangutans could be killed, injured or displaced.
Wildfires happen every year in Indonesia, where fire is often used to clear land to make way for palm or pulp plantations. But the arrival of a supercharged El Niño has brought especially dry conditions, causing blazes to spread rapidly across parts of Sumatra, Kalimantan (the Indonesian part of Borneo) and Papua.
The fires have also taken hold across peatland, which is extremely hard to extinguish as it smoulders underground. In its natural state, it should be waterlogged, but over recent decades, vast areas have been drained by industrial agriculture, leaving it highly flammable.
Habitat containing 52% of the total Bornean orangutan population is now affected by the fires, according to a statement from the IUCN’s primate specialists.
They are not the only animals affected, however. Blazes have also spread into the habitats of five gibbon species, all of which are listed as endangered on the IUCN Red List. Geopix, an environmental NGO, warned earlier this month that 4,500 fires had been detected across 21 Sumatran elephant habitats over recent months.

Swiss glaciers have suffered a near-record loss of ice in 2026, new data shows, as intense summer heatwaves take their toll on Alpine peaks.
More than 5% of the country's remaining glacier ice has disappeared in the last 12 months, which scientists say is "extraordinary".
They warn that such rapid melting is no longer a surprise given the pace of climate change, but it could threaten water supplies for farming, hydropower and transport in the decades ahead.
The loss of glacier ice can also destabilise mountain slopes and increase the risk of landslides in some places - which can lead to flash flooding in extreme cases, as seen in Nepal in August.
There were multiple factors involved in that event, which was triggered when a large area of bedrock and glacier ice collapsed. 
But scientists say long-term glacier thinning and the thawing of frozen ground likely raised the risks.
The notable finding from this latest report is not so much that Swiss glaciers are shrinking - which is to be expected in our warming climate, driven primarily by fossil fuel emissions - but the sheer pace of melting. 
Until recently, glaciologists in the Alps considered 2% of ice lost in a single year to be "extreme". This year has seen an estimated 5.5% disappear.














"It's really just disastrous," said Dr Matthias Huss, director of Glacier Monitoring Switzerland, which produced the report.



Swiss glaciers started the summer in an already difficult place, covered by less snow than usual after a mild winter.
And much of that snow disappeared quickly in the early and intense heatwaves of May and June, exposing the glacier ice below.
Bare ice is darker and less reflective than fresh snow, so absorbs more of the Sun's energy. 
That left glaciers vulnerable to melting even faster in subsequent heatwaves.
"Ten years ago, I wouldn't have thought that it's possible to lose glaciers so quickly," said Dr Fabien Maussion, a glaciologist at the University of Bristol, who was not involved in the Swiss report.
"What's happened over the summer now is extremely distressing… but at the same time it was to be expected from a climate scientist's perspective," he added.







Meltwater from glaciers can be an important source of water for irrigation, hydropower and even shipping traffic during hot, dry conditions. 
Scientists estimate that Swiss glaciers released 2.2 trillion litres of meltwater between July and September.
Although that helped to ease water shortages this summer, it has rapidly diminished the frozen supply. 
The loss of ice could pose long-term challenges, Huss warned, with smaller glaciers unable to top up water levels to the same extent.
"Every drop of water that runs off during these heatwaves is kind of old water that's been stocked in the glacier ice centuries or decades ago," said Huss.
"It's helping us [now] but it's unsustainable, so we won't have it at [our] disposal in the next heatwave."

New UK gas and oil projects are a ‘no-brainer’, says EDF boss


Developing North Sea fields does not contradict net zero goals, according to Simone Rossi




New oil and gas projects are a “no-brainer” that pose “no contradiction” to the net zero agenda, according to the head of EDF Energy.
Simone Rossi has joined a string of renewables leaders in making the case for more North Sea production as the government prepares to decide on two projects there.

He said ministers should give the Rosebank and Jackdaw fields the green light, while accelerating support for heat pumps and electric vehicles.
“It will take decades to wean off from that dependency,” Rossi said in an interview with the BBC. “So while this is happening we should use the resources that we’ve got rather than importing them from afar. For me, it’s really a no-brainer. It is not in contradiction.”


View image in fullscreen
Simone Rossi, the chief executive of EDF Energy, says UK oil and gas projects have lower emissions than imports. Photograph: PA Images/Alamy Stock Photo/Alamy Live News.
New North Sea developments would help to create jobs and increase government tax receipts that could be used to support households struggling to pay energy bills, according to Rossi.


He said locally produced fossil fuels had lower emissions than imports because they do not need to transported over long distances.
“In the UK the only way we can reduce emissions is to genuinely reduce the usage of fossil fuels at the point of use,” he said. “Over time, the only solution is electricity.”
The boss of EDF Energy, which generates about a fifth of the UK’s low-carbon electricity, has become the latest high-profile advocate of climate action to also make a case for more North Sea production. Others include: Greg Jackson, the founder of Octopus Energy; Jürgen Maier, the former boss of GB Energy; and Tara Singh, the boss of RenewableUK.

Communities across California are rushing to prepare for the imminent arrival of the so-called “Kelvin wave”, a massive underwater band of warm water threatening to inundate swaths of the vast North American shoreline.
The wave is nearing southern California and expected to reach the San Francisco Bay Area by early October, as it crawls toward Alaska. Waters could rise by a foot along the California coast, according to scientists, who have warned that this could dramatically double the 8-12in rise in sea levels already caused by climate change over the last century.

The Kelvin wave doesn’t climb and crash like a typical ocean wave; rather, it swells the tides from beneath the surface. It’s effectively a massive slosh of warm water, driven by El Niño conditions, that moves across the Pacific before colliding with the South American coastline and surging north. It also won’t transport water in the way a tsunami might, but creates conditions that enable higher sea levels to linger.
On their own, Kelvin waves aren’t always hazardous, according to Mike Jacox, a research oceanographer with the National Marine Fisheries Service, though they can reduce the growth of phytoplankton that form the base of the marine food web. “But when there are very high tides or storm surges, their effects can be amplified,” he said.


If the rising waters coincide with other climatic events, such as rainstorms and high tides, the phenomenon could swallow beaches, chew away bluffs and coastlines, and submerge streets, homes and businesses.

For many vertebrates, insects are more than a food source. As “little things that run the world”, insects provide critical functions such as protection, sanitation and shelter across ecosystems, according to a new study.
The study, published in Nature Reviews Biodiversity on Wednesday, sheds light on the various ways insects support vertebrates, ranging from birds and bats to reptiles, amphibians and mammals.

Nearly three-quarters of terrestrial and freshwater vertebrates eat invertebrates, according to the paper, with insects frequently making up a large portion of their diets.
However, their relationship goes beyond predator and prey.







Scientists are fighting a longer mosquito season with ... more mosquitoes

Read more
The paper, led by Eliza Grames, an assistant professor of biological sciences at Binghamton University, State University of New York, documents dozens of less obvious ways vertebrates depend on the estimated 14m to 30m species of insects found around the world.
Chimpanzees, for example, have been recorded applying insects to treat open wounds, while more than 200 bird species use ants to remove parasites or maintain feathers. Other birds build nests near wasps or other stinging insects, in a likely effort to gain protection from predators.
Insects also provide shelter, the study notes. Birds, reptiles and mammals use termite mounds and ant nests, which can offer stable temperatures and humidity. White-throated round-eared bats, for instance, excavate cavities in termite mounds and use them as roosts.


Other insects act as sanitation workers. Dung beetles remove animal waste and can make dung drier and more aerated, in turn reducing parasite survival, according to the study. Meanwhile, moths living in some bird nests consume feces, feathers and other debris. The review notes that insects have performed similar functions for millions of years, citing evidence of beetles feeding on feathers in dinosaur nests during the Cretaceous period, which lasted from around 145m to 66m years ago.
Other insect-vertebrate relationships include beetles removing ectoparasites from rodents and snakes feeding on firefly larvae to obtain defensive toxins, as well as antbirds using live crickets during courtship.
Mutually beneficial relationships also occur across the insect-vertebrate realm, with sloths relying on moths to deposit nitrogen in their fur and spur algal growth, which the sloths then eat. Sloths then descend from trees once a month to defecate on the ground, providing substrate in which moths lay eggs.
According to the study, such overlooked relationships could become increasingly important as insect communities evolve. Although the extent of insect declines varies across habitats and regions, the review says that “widespread and considerable disruption” of insect communities is “inevitable” as land use changes.


Grames called the study a “wake-up call for anyone concerned about the biodiversity crisis”.

I heard one thing loud and clear in Andy Burnham’s landmark speech: the left has won the arguments

Owen Jones






The PM’s stated trajectory is a rebuke to past Tory and Labour governments. The challenge now is to make his project progressive in word and deed





As Andy Burnham delivered his conference speech to the Labour faithful yesterday, it was hard not to recall Jeremy Corbyn’s words after the party’s shattering 2019 election defeat. “I am proud that on austerity, on corporate power, on inequality and the climate emergency,” he wrote for this publication, “we have won the arguments and rewritten the terms of political debate.” Given Boris Johnson’s 80-seat majority, widespread mockery ensued.
But when it comes to rhetoric, who can now deny that the left has won the argument? A Labour prime minister has declared that “Britain has been on the wrong path for a long time”, listing five villains: “Deindustrialisation, deregulation, privatisation, austerity, Brexit.” His speech was infused with class politics, as he condemned a society “run for vested interests, not in the public interest, with power held in too few hands”.



When he committed to break with the “flawed thinking of the last 40 years”, he lumped together Conservative and Labour governments. He has already repeatedly labelled the culprit: neoliberalism. This has long been the received wisdom of the left: that as Clement Attlee’s postwar government established a social-democratic consensus that the Tories upheld for a generation, so Margaret Thatcher bequeathed a settlement that New Labour maintained.
These beliefs were condemned to the fringes of Labour, even though Tony Blair himself eventually confessed: “I always thought my job was to build on some of the things she had done rather than reverse them.” Any mention of neoliberalism was a sure way of provoking an eye-roll from a mainstream politician or commentator. We were denied any debate about an economic system based on extraction rather than investment; an economy based on financialisation rather than making things. World’s oceans absorbed record heat equal to 40 times annual global energy use


The injection of thermal energy comes amid an increasing rise in sea levels and continuing acidification




A record-breaking 23 zettajoules of heat was sunk into the world’s seas last year, leaving ocean waters hotter, higher and less hospitable, a report has found.
The explosive addition of thermal energy, which was almost 40 times greater than all the energy humanity used that year, comes amid far-reaching changes to the deep water bodies fundamental to life on Earth.

Sea levels have risen by about 3.8mm per year since 1999, and at a faster rate of 4.2mm per year between 2012 and 2025, according to the 10th edition of the Copernicus ocean state report. It found the global ocean has become 17% more acidic in the last 40 years.







What are zettajoules – and what do they tell us about Earth’s energy imbalance?

Read more
Oceans have absorbed about one-third of the carbon dioxide that humanity has spewed and about 90% of the extra heat that greenhouse gas pollution has trapped in the Earth’s system.
“The ocean is transforming before our eyes,” said Pierre Bahurel, director general of Mercator Ocean International, which published the report. “Warming, rising seas and ecosystem degradation are interconnected signs of significant and long-term change.”
In Europe, which is heating twice as fast as the global average, the Mediterranean and Black Seas have been plagued by record-breaking marine heatwaves – with elevated temperatures that persist deep below the surface – and bouts of extreme heat that have lasted more than a month, the scientists found.


View image in fullscreen
A Mediterranean swimmer in mid-January: the entire sea has warmed by .32C per decade. Photograph: Hassan Ammar/AP
The scientists found a clear acceleration of sea level rise in the western Mediterranean, even as the eastern part showed uneven gains. The entire sea has warmed by 0.32C per decade, the report found, driving up marine heatwaves, particularly in the last few years. A joule, the unit used to measure heat, is the amount of electricity required to run a one watt device for one second; a zettajoule is a billion trillion joules.


The report comes as western Europe experiences an unusually warm September right after its ruinously fiery summer, with temperatures hitting 40C highs in parts of Spain and Portugal last week. Hot coastal waters exacerbate heatwaves on land by adding heat during nights that would otherwise cool down.

Southern areas are likely to see the highest temperatures, but the warmer weather is expected to be felt generally across the UK, with most places experiencing above-average temperatures for September.

More than a hundred invasive species may colonise coastal waters worldwide by mid-century as sea levels rise due to climate change, a new study warns.
Invasive species like Chinese mitten crabs, Pacific oysters, and Asian tiger shrimps can lead to biodiversity loss and ecosystem change, with devastating economic impacts.
While previous studies have shown that climate change can alter species distributions on land and at sea, the impact of invasive, non-native marine species entering newly flooded areas due to the rise in sea levels has remained unclear.




“Sea-level rise may open new habitats for the landward expansion of marine non-native species into inundated coastal lands, which remains unexplored,” the latest study, published in Nature Ecology & Evolution, explains. 
Estuaries are particularly vulnerable to invasive marine species, it notes, as they are hubs of human activity.

The research models the future distribution of 122 non-native marine species, including the European green crab, the northern Pacific sea star, the bamboo worm and the pleated sea squirt under scenarios of continued sea-level rise. A scenario of moderate carbon emissions will see the global sea level rise by an average of 20cm by 2050.


In this scenario, the study predicts that between 290,000 and 470,000 sq km of inundated coastal land, almost the size of Italy, will become suitable habitat for invasive species, which often possess traits that give them competitive advantages over native species.
Invasive species like the Pacific oyster, the Atlantic blue crab, the predatory snail Veined rapa whelk, and the Asian tiger shrimp could colonise two-thirds of inundated coastal land in regions where they are already established.


Some of the marine creatures covered in the study, such as the striped barnacle, the orange-striped green sea anemone, the Indo-Pacific swimming crab, are expected to gain the most habitat from the inundated area. They are likely to spread most extensively in areas close to estuaries.

UN warns of ‘narrowing window’ to restore world’s forests


Food and Agriculture Organization urges governments to make forest restoration a national priority 




The world faces a “narrowing window” to restore forests essential for food security and resistance to the climate emergency, a United Nations report has warned.
More than 489m hectares (1.2bn acres) of forests have been cleared since 1990, while an even greater area is degraded, the world body said in a call for governments to make forest restoration a national priority.

The State of the World’s Forests report acknowledges recent steps forward in protection and tree planting around the globe but says action has not kept pace with commitments.
Over the past two decades, national, regional and global initiatives have promised to place more than 1bn hectares of land under restoration, but barely a fifth of that is actually being restored, the report by the UN Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) notes, saying: “Progress is uneven, and it is insufficient to meet growing global needs.”

Forests, which cover 4.14bn hectares (about a third of Earth’s land surface), store 714 gigatonnes of carbon and host up to 80% of the world’s terrestrial biodiversity. They also play an important role in regulating rainfall and in reducing hunger, with nearly one-third of the global population depending on them for livelihoods.


Threats are intensifying. Every year, about 127m hectares of forest are affected by fires, with further damage caused by insects, diseases and severe weather events. This is making forests ever more vulnerable, as it comes on top of pressure from farm expansion, the climate crisis, pollution and the extraction of fossil fuels and other resources.

“This widening gap between demand and sustainable supply highlights a structural imbalance that threatens both ecological integrity and the long-term viability of forest-based economies,” the report states.
It says remedial action on forests and other degraded ecosystems would benefit people, food security and the economy – with restoration of 1bn hectares estimated to generate $1.8tn in benefits each year.

The Trump administration on Monday announced it was slashing clean car rules that had been aimed at reducing planet-heating emissions and boosting electric vehicles.
The move, which was criticized by environmentalists, relaxes requirements on automakers to control pollution from gasoline-powered cars and light trucks for model years 2022 through 2031.

The new rule, announced by the Department of Transportation, reverses a push by the Biden administration to accelerate the transition to EVs. Transportation is the largest source of climate emissions in the United States, accounting for about 28% of total US greenhouse gas emissions according to the US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA).
Monday’s move follows the Trump administration’s rollback of the government’s ability to impose requirements to track, report and limit climate-heating pollution from cars and trucks.



Donald Trump said on Truth Social on Saturday that the less stringent mileage requirements would “take the waste out of building cars in America” and save families “thousands on a new, beautiful and safe car”, while boosting auto production in the US.
Trump has repeatedly pledged to end what he falsely calls an EV “mandate”, referring incorrectly to Joe Biden’s target that half of all new vehicle sales be electric by 2030. No federal policy has mandated auto companies to sell EVs.
Sean Duffy, the US transportation secretary, hailed the new initiative – called Freedom Means Affordable Cars – which the agency said would reduce the average cost of new vehicles by $1,300, and save consumers $138bn over the next five years.
Duffy said: “Thanks to President Trump’s leadership, we have finally ended the illegal mandate that forced automakers to produce more expensive electric vehicles that American families didn’t want.”
Green groups condemned the new rules. Dan Becker, director of the Center for Biological Diversity’s safe climate transport campaign, said that the final rule “ignores the feasibility of clean technology and the millions of fuel-efficient cars already on the road”.

Katherine García, director of the Sierra Club’s Clean transportation for all campaign, vowed the environmental group would fight the rule and said that the loosening of fuel standards would “make driving more expensive too”.

Londoners should brace themselves for icy weather and freezing temperatures as El Niño threatens to wreak havoc on weather once again this year. 




The weather phenomenon saw the capital face its hottest summer on record as wildfires and drought swept over the UK. 








But the worst could be yet to come with experts warning of a wet and stormy winter - and even a polar vortex - as the strongest El Niño event in 1,000 years develops over the Pacific Ocean. 


People shelter from the rain under an umbrella, in Westminster, central London (Jonathan Brady/PA)
PA Wire




It comes as government bodies and experts urge Britons to start stockpiling food and water in case of an emergency. Defence Secretary Wes Streeting has advised that all homes should have cash, a supply of bottled water, and some tinned goods at their disposal should disaster strike, the Sun reported. 




El Niño is a naturally occurring climate cycle which takes place when sea temperatures become warmer than average, impacting air circulation patterns. This year’s El Niño has been dubbed “Godzilla” because of its exceptional impact and scale. 




As early as this week, rainy, gusty and stormy weather could blow over London and the UK. 




The Met Office has warned that there could be an increased likelihood of spells of rain and strong winds in comparison to average during parts of the season in London, but it is “not possible to attribute specific weather events to El Niño”. 




Meteorologists have also warned of a polar vortex - a large band of counter-clockwise winds that circle above the Earth’s North and South poles. 











The stratospheric polar vortex is not a weather system that moves into the UK, but changes in its strength could influence weather patterns lower down in the atmosphere, according to forecasters.




A spokesperson for the Met Office said: “A stronger-than-normal polar vortex can favour a stronger jet stream, which may increase the likelihood of mild, wet and windy conditions. 









“Conversely, a weaker polar vortex can sometimes increase the chances of colder weather affecting the UK.” 




Dan Holley, Met Office deputy chief forecaster, told the Independent that a “deep area of low pressure could pass close to the UK” this week.

Concern mounts over slow-moving, planetary-scale ‘Kelvin’ wave heading for California


The ocean phenomenon could raise sea levels by up to a foot as El Niño keeps warm water trapped along the coast




Concerns are mounting about an ocean phenomenon known as a Kelvin wave that could raise sea levels along the California coastline by up to a foot, as scientists say El Niño is supercharging the threat of storm surges and flooding in the coming months.
As an incredibly strong El Niño continues to develop in the Pacific, the phenomenon brings with it a strange shift in the ocean. The Kelvin wave phenomenon is created when trade winds that usually blow from South America towards Asia die down or reverse in El Niño years, setting off a massive, slow-moving slosh of water.

Kelvin waves are not like crashing waves at the beach. They are planetary in scale, spanning thousands of miles. And when a Kelvin wave kicks off, it brings with it an untold amount of warm water that slowly moves from the western Pacific, along the equator, towards South, Central and North America.


“You can follow them along … we see the higher sea levels along the equator, and when the wave reaches the coast of South America, it cannot continue to go eastward,” Severine Fournier, a research scientist studying ocean circulation at Nasa’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory, said. “So it goes north and south.”
One such wave hit the northern tip of South America in late August and has begun moving up towards the west coast of the US. That wave could reach California shores within days, and when it does, ocean scientists say it may raise sea levels by up to a foot for months as El Niño lingers and keeps that warm water trapped along the coast.
Nate Mantua, a research scientist at the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration’s Southwest Fisheries Science Center, explained that in a typical year, there is a thick layer of warm water in the western Pacific.
“When the wind stops blowing or weakens, the force that’s holding that pile of water in place goes away, so that water surges or sloshes back towards California,” he said, noting researchers expect the influence of the Kelvin wave to linger through the winter and into early next year.
Mantua said Kelvin waves were a natural phenomenon that have been happening for thousands of years and measured by agencies like Noaa since record-keeping began. But sea levels have already risen about 8in over the last century, meaning Kelvin waves will add more water on top of a figure that’s already going up.


“We can predict a lot of the impacts,” he added, “but not all.”

An oil-like substance has been bubbling up in the River Avon in Bristol for years and killing wildlife, according to local residents who have made regular reports to the Environment Agency (EA).

"We continue to work with landowners, the local authority and partner organisations to take action to protect the local environment."

Firms manipulating process to avoid emission controls and scrutiny of their projects, environmental groups warn




Datacenter developers are manipulating the EPA’s air pollution permitting process to avoid emission controls and scrutiny of their projects, environmental advocates allege.
Companies need federal permits to emit a range of pollutants. In their permit applications, some in big tech are avoiding “major” reviews by dividing their emissions sources into separate, multiple “minor” sources that require less regulatory oversight, the advocates say.

Read more
This helps datacenters avoid public scrutiny, and permit applications are typically approved much faster. It also likely saves tech companies money, and avoids the hassle and cost of potential pollution controls, advocates say. Datacenters can be significant sources of nitrogen oxide, ozone, heavy metals, particulate matter, greenhouse gas and other dangerous air pollutants.
In North Carolina, Amazon and utility giant Duke Energy are installing 649 diesel generators to back up a new hyperscale center. They submitted two permits, and avoided a major review despite being in a low income area that already suffers from high levels of air pollution.
In New Mexico, the Project Jupiter datacenter developers attempted to circumvent a major review by proposing two natural gas “microgrids” for either side of the facility and submitting two “minor” permits. The overall project would have released enough pollution to trigger a major review.


In Frederick, Maryland, four datacenters with separate minor permits, including one by Amazon, operate on a single campus with a master developer, regulatory documents show. In other instances, data center developers have staggered minor permit requests over months that cumulatively emit as much pollution as a major source, advocates say.
These regulatory maneuvers make it less clear how much pollution residents living near the facilities are exposed to, and the move amounts to “lego permitting”, said Michael Koerber, a retired deputy director of the EPA’s Office of Air Quality Planning and Standards, which worked on permitting.

Coastal erosion has been eating away at the beach in San Clemente, known for nearly a century as a “Spanish village by the sea.” The rising sea and crashing waves have pushed the shoreline landward, splitting the city's picturesque North Beach. It's one of many California coastal communities grappling with the effects of sea level rise. Nearly a decade ago, scientists forecast that more than half of Southern California’s beaches could significantly erode by 2100, radically altering how people live and recreate along the state’s famed coast.

A month on from Nepal’s devastating floods, the disaster looks set to pile billions of pounds onto the country’s national debt burden – as experts warn it could become the latest country to face a huge debt bill from a climate crisis it has done little to cause.
On 26 August, more than 100 million cubic metres of rock and glacier broke away from Langtang Lirung mountain on Nepal’s northern border, triggering a 188km/h debris flood that buried villages, changed the course of rivers, and killed more than 1,400 people.
Scientists have since said that the event was made significantly more likely due to climate change, while the finance minister has warned that the final death toll could exclude that of a devastating 2015 earthquake. 




A subsequent rapid assessment of damage from the Nepali government has put the cost of recovery and reconstruction at $4.8 billion (£3.6bn) – equivalent to 11 per cent of the country’s GDP – and government figures have called for grant-based compensation as a matter of ‘climate justice’, given the fact that Nepal contributes to an estimated 0.1 per cent of greenhouse gas emissions each year. 





open image in gallery
Nepal suffered one of the worst catastrophes in its history when a tsunami-like flood cut a swathe of destruction claiming more than 1,400 lives and leaving 5,000 unaccounted for (AFP/Getty)
But the Fund for responding to Loss and Damage, established at the UN climate summit COP27 in Egypt in 2022, has so far secured just $822m in pledges, of which only $456m has actually been paid in, limiting the scale of support available to countries hit by disasters.

The fact that applications for withdrawals are limited to only $20m per country means the government will likely be forced to foot the bill with public debt, according to experts. 


“The loss and damage fund was created to support countries facing unprecedented climate disasters such as this, but it has nowhere near enough money,” says Ritu Bharadwaj, director of climate resilience at the International Institute for Environment and Development (IIED). 
“Even if - by a stroke of luck - they received the $20m they can apply for, that is less than half of a percent of the $4.8bn in damages.”


Bharadwaj continues: “Right now, there is still media attention. But once that goes, Nepal will be left to fend for itself - and that will mean borrowing huge amounts of money at an expensive rate, leaving the country at the mercy of creditors who can essentially use debt to control the country in an almost colonial manner.”

articles.raw_rss: Divisions in the party are rising over closer ties with Europe
articles.raw_content:
Labour has blocked a debate on whether to have closer ties with Europe at its annual conference next week as splits in the party widen over the scope of the Brexit reset.



The official reason for blocking the motion calling on the party to drop its blanket opposition to rejoining the single market, customs union or free movement of people is that it is not a “contemporary ” issue.



But insiders claim this party jargon really means the issue is “too sensitive”.





It comes as speculation increases over how far Andy Burnham will go in redrawing the UK’s relationship with Europe after he refused to rule out committing to rejoining the EU in the next Labour manifesto.



Overtures from Europe



The Government’s Brexit reset – which was on the verge of being signed by Sir Keir Starmer – is faltering amid a negotiating deadlock on a youth mobility or exchange scheme and UK demands that the UK should not be shut out of new “Made in Europe” laws.



These will dictate that public contracts within the EU favour companies based in the bloc. It is designed to counter cheap Chinese products, particularly clean technology and electric vehicles.



The debate was then turbocharged by former prime minister Sir Tony Blair, who called on his party to commit to rejoining within a decade. Unions earlier this month called on Labour to drop its red lines.



The i Paper also reported overtures from European Parliament Brexit chief Sandro Gozi for the UK to pursue a closer deal with the EU

articles.title: The treasured 'eternal snow' on this tropical island is about to disappear forever
articles.raw_rss: Climate change is transforming Papua's snowy peaks, which hold scientific value and spiritual significance.
articles.raw_meta: Climate change is transforming Papua's snowy peaks, which hold scientific value and spiritual significance.
articles.jina_text:
The peaks in this Indonesian region on the world's second-largest island, just north of Australia, have offered scientists countless insights into the Earth's climate history.
They're also the epicentre of the spiritual universe for many Papuans - a Mecca or a Vatican, as one activist puts it.
But now, nearly all the snow is gone.
A century ago, the 300km (190-mile) stretch of the Sudirman Range had snow and permanent ice on all four of its major peaks.
But now there are only small areas around Puncak Jaya, also known as Carstensz Pyramid, with any snow at all. These are expected to entirely disappear in a year or two.
Glacier cover around the peak has shrunk from nearly 1,900 hectares (4,700 acres) in the 19th Century to about 16 hectares (40 acres) today. Almost entire glaciers have vanished within a human lifetime.









"There is a profound unfairness in this," says Marie Šabacká, a Czech glacier ecologist who travelled to Puncak Jaya last March in a bid to be among the last scientists to study Papua's "eternal snow".
She says the tropical glaciers in Papua are unique because they are separated from other glacier systems by thousands of kilometres. Papua is home to the "last remaining tropical ice" between the Andes and Himalayas.
Ice cores taken from the slopes of Puncak Jaya preserve a record of climate history. 
Scientists can use them to obtain information about atmospheric conditions in the region and understand changes in the planet's warmest ocean waters that surround the island - the tropical Pacific and Western Pacific Warm pool.
But this archive is disappearing before scientists have had time to fully study it.





Image caption, 

The snow cover has reduced dramatically since this photo, taken in 1936



Proof of a warming planet




The retreat of Papua's glaciers is driven by the same forces affecting ice around the world, Šabacká notes, a warming atmosphere caused by human activity, including the burning of fossil fuels like coal, oil and gas.
As temperatures rise, the freezing point moves higher up mountains, so more precipitation falls as rain instead of snow, even in places that once saw regular snowfall.
El Niño events can accelerate this process, while local factors such as cloud cover, snowfall and mountain topography influence its pace.
The mountains in Papua are just 450km (280 miles) south of the equator, where "permanent ice can survive only at very high altitudes and within a narrow range of climatic conditions", Šabacká says.
A small increase in temperature, a higher freezing point or shift from snowfall to rainfall can determine whether a glacier survives at all, she adds.
The glaciers' retreat is evidence the Earth has been warming over a long period - and their disappearance "removes both a biological habitat and part of a culturally significant landscape".

articles.jina_text:
Hurricanes Lala in August and Lowell in early September flooded homes and roads, downed trees and toppled electricity lines across the islands. Nolo, which strengthened to a hurricane on Thursday night, is expected to batter the islands with rain and high surf.

Despite its location, stretching across roughly 1,500 miles in the central north Pacific Ocean, Hawaii typically avoids the worst effects from hurricanes. In fact, the island chain so often dodges direct hits from the violent storms that it’s been quipped they have a force field around them.
But the islands have seen an unusual amount of severe storms this year. Already, more than 500 homes have been damaged or destroyed as Nolo threatens to unleash downpours that could measure in feet instead of inches.


“An event of this magnitude is somewhat rare,” Michael Brennan, director of the National Hurricane Center, said during a broadcast discussion as Lowell swirled closer last month, adding that Hawaii has not had a direct hurricane landfall since Iniki in 1992. That violent storm unleashed 145 mile-per-hour winds as it tore through Kauai, destroying or damaging roughly 70% of the island’s homes and businesses.


It’s not luck (or a force field) that typically protected the islands, but location, according to Dr Nicholas Grondin, assistant professor of environmental science at the University of Tampa. Among the most isolated chains of islands on Earth, Hawaii is simply a small target in the vast open ocean, Grondin explained in an editorial published by the Conversation.
Most approaching storms also must pass over cooler water temperatures to the east of the islands, which helps calm them. “Without warm oceans to provide fuel, hurricanes tend to weaken and fizzle out as they approach the islands,” Grondin said.
Sea-surface temperatures in the tropical Pacific are, however, exceptionally warm this year due to El Niño. The climate phenomenon typically limits hurricane activity in the Atlantic and enhances the development and strength of storms in the Pacific. El Niño has already developed, but is expected to strengthen through the coming months, and forecasters have warned there is a high probability it will reach a historic intensity.
El Niño has caused hurricanes to form further to the south and west this year, according to Matthew Rosencrans, National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration’s lead forecaster for the seasonal hurricane outlook, which “puts them in a place where they could make that westward run towards the Hawaiian islands”.


It also makes for a lagging storm season. Hurricane risks typically extend from July to the end of November but fall off into the later months. September and October are far busier in El Niño years.
The climate crisis has also played a part in strengthening the storms. The effects of El Niño are layered on top of the warming trends.

Powered by sun and wind, the uncrewed vehicle will collect data to help Australian scientists better understand how oceans absorb emissions 
 
 
Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast 




A small uncrewed vessel has embarked on a lap around Antarctica and may not return for months.
The seven-metre craft, which looks like a large kayak in hi-vis orange, is expected to travel about 22,000km through inhospitable waters, propelled by powerful westerly winds and energy from the sun. The journey is seven times the distance between Sydney and Perth.

Along the way, it is expected to encounter massive waves, freezing temperatures, ferocious winds, and even the odd curious seal or albatross.
The mission? To collect data on carbon dioxide in the ocean and atmosphere, to help scientists better understand the role of ocean sinks.

Dr Elizabeth Shadwick, a principal research scientist at the CSIRO, said that after leaving Hobart the vessel would travel east towards New Zealand, “eventually scooching through the Drake Passage between the bottom of South America and Antarctica, then coming along past South Africa and back to us here, where we’ll pick it up.”
She hoped to see it again in seven to nine months.


View image in fullscreen
The vessel has a heavy keel to keep it upright and a solar sail to power it. Photograph: CSIRO AAPP
The autonomous vehicle made by the US maritime company Saildrone was designed to withstand the intrepid voyage, with a heavy keel keeping it upright, a rudder to steer and a fixed solar sail poking above the surface. It would be remotely monitored by the company, who would check in regularly via satellite, and, if necessary, nudge it in the right direction.


“It’s already been bashed around pretty heavily,” Shadwick said. “It’s quite a robust little device. We saw some eight metres of waves just the day after we deployed it and a 35-knot wind.”
Measurements taken throughout its journey – including wind speed, atmospheric pressure, solar radiation, ocean temperature, salinity and chlorophyll, as well as carbon dioxide levels in the water and air – were expected to assist scientists in better understanding the role that oceans play in global heating.

Freezing temperatures and unsettled conditions could sweep the UK as the El Niño weather phenomenon continues to wreak havoc on global weather.
Experts are predicting a wet and stormy autumn that could develop into an icy winter after the “super El Niño” smashed global benchmarks to become the strongest event in history.
The Met Office said the “unprecedented” phenomenon, which has already helped push temperatures to reach the hottest summer on record, will continue to have “far-reaching” implications for weather conditions across the world.





El Niño is a naturally occurring climate phenomenon that develops in the tropical Pacific Ocean. It takes place when sea-surface temperatures across the central and eastern Pacific become significantly warmer than average, altering atmospheric circulation patterns and influencing weather around the globe.

An energy efficient home can not only reduce your mortgage payments and your bills – it also increases the value of your property. articles.jina_text:
More tree planting, wetland restoration and drainage work could take place in parts of Northamptonshire to "safeguard nature for generations to come". 
West Northamptonshire Council has approved its first Local Nature Recovery Strategy (LNRS) which was required by the Environment Act 2021 and is the responsibility of all authorities.
It said the area was one of England's "most nature-depleted areas" and its wildlife sites "are often small, in poor condition, and isolated from one another".
Working with a range of partners the council hopes to improve landscapes that are "under unprecedented pressure" with some species in decline.
A spokesperson for the council said: "A healthy natural environment is essential for tackling climate change and wider environmental challenges. 
"The diversity of habitats and species provide essentials such as clean and plentiful water, food, clean air, productive soil, flood protection, shading and cooling, as well as benefits like space for recreation, exercise and wellbeing."
Nigel Stansfield, Reform UK's cabinet member for environment, recycling and waste, said: "Our aim is to safeguard nature for generations to come, and create cleaner, greener spaces that meet the needs of local communities and offer them an opportunity to connect with nature."
He said it was vital to have a workable strategy that sets out "how we intend to safeguard nature for generations to come."
Stansfield added he hoped the strategy would get organisations, landowners and local people to take action "to ensure our natural environment becomes more robust and resilient to provide the benefits we often take for granted".

“Gospić is our home,” Željka Šikić shouted to a crowd of 40,000 people outside the Croatian parliament earlier this month. The slogan is the name of a campaign she helped to set up to protest against the illegal dumping of waste in Gospić, a town in the mountainous Lika region of central Croatia.
Between 2022 and 2024, waste was illegally abandoned at several sites in the town. At one of the biggest, just 50 metres from Šikić’s home, an estimated 35,000 tonnes of waste, some of it hazardous, was dumped and buried.

In the dead of night, lorries heaving with waste would pass her front door and enter a nearby industrial site. This activity went largely unnoticed by the local authorities and police. But residents in Gospić were well aware and started taking it in turns to stay up to photograph the vehicles coming in and out of the site.
“I don’t think it should be our job to stay awake all night to see what’s going on,” Šikić says.


View image in fullscreen
An illegal waste site in Gospić in August. Photograph: Pixsell/Alamy
The waste became a blight on the community and a recent report from the Croatian Institute of Public Health revealed Pfas “forever chemicals” had been detected in groundwater samples nearby. Elevated concentrations of copper and lead were also detected in the soil.


Pfas are a group of thousands of synthetic chemicals that have been linked to serious health conditions, including several types of cancer. They are known as “forever chemicals” because of how long they persist in the environment.
Despite assurances that their drinking water is safe, a lack of trust means many residents have resorted to buying bottled water.
“I’m really scared,” Šikić says. “I would like to move house but I don’t know who would pay for the house on the first road next to the waste. I feel betrayed.”


View image in fullscreen
Residents took to filming lorries going in and out of one of the dumping sites on the outskirts of Gospić, seen here last month. Photograph: Pixsell/Alamy
In February 2025, years after the activity began, police and law enforcement officers arrested 13 people on suspicion of being part of the environmental criminal network involved in dumping the waste.
The main suspects, two Croatian nationals, were considered high-value targets by Europol and were believed to have orchestrated the illegal import of hazardous waste from Italy, Slovenia and Germany. It is thought the criminals generated upwards of €4m (£3.4m) in profit from this activity.


Waste crime is big business. Criminal networks often take advantage of the high costs associated with treating and disposing of waste properly. By falsifying documents to declare the waste as destined for recycling, they can save on the costs and pocket the difference.
Residents in Gospić had hoped the arrests would finally mean the site was shut down and cleaned up. But 18 months later, it is still there.

Ms Chaffe’s “tenancy for life” deal means that the Labour-run Hammersmith and Fulham Council cannot kick her out, and have an obligation to maintain it.




She moved into the house in 1995, claiming they had separated, and Hamza’s eight children were raised in the property.




Three of his sons have since served jail sentences for offences related to drugs, money laundering and fraud.

Hamza, the hook-handed former imam of Finsbury Park Mosque, never officially lived at the address but was seen there on a number of occasions before his first arrest in 2004.

The UK faced its hottest summer on record this year, with much of the country experiencing drought and repeated heatwaves.
But temperatures and rainfall were not the same everywhere. Type in your postcode to see what summer 2026 was like in your area.



  
 
 
 
 
 
🏠🌤️ How was summer 2026 near you? 
A modern browser with JavaScript and a stable internet connection is required to view this interactive. 
As a result, we can't show information for your location, but data for the entire UK is available below.  
Data up to August 2026   
☀️ Temperature 
In the UK summer temperatures have been above average. 
The maximum daily temperature was 21.3C on average, which is 2.4C above what it was for summer between 1991 and 2020. 
Virtually all of the UK experienced above average temperatures, driven by repeated heatwaves. 
Southern England and Wales saw heat far above usual. Temperatures were closer to normal across Scotland and Northern Ireland. 
 
    
Average daily maximum in summer 2026 compared with the 1991-2020 average  
 
Average daily maximum temperature map key 
 
Colder: blue 
Warmer: red  
 
 
-4C: deepest blue 
No Change: white 
+4C: deepest red       
🌧️ Rainfall 
Rainfall in the UK has been below average this summer. 
Across the country a total of 195mm of rain fell on average, which is 23% below what it was for summer between 1991 and 2020. 
Summer months tend to be drier, but this year was exceptional. Only north-western Scotland saw more summer rain than usual, as droughts were declared across much of the rest of the UK. 
 
    
Total rainfall in summer 2026 as a percentage of 1991-2020 average summer rainfall  
 
Total rainfall map key 
 
Drier: brown 
Wetter: blue  
 
 
-100%: deepest brown 
No Change: white 
+100%: deepest blue          
About the data  
 
Where does the data come from? 
This lookup uses data from the HadUK Grid dataset     (opens in new tab), which is produced by the Met Office Hadley Centre. HadUK Grid is one of the main products used by scientists to monitor and research the UK’s changing climate. 
The HadUK dataset displays temperature and rainfall data across a uniform grid covering the entire landmass of the UK. The data does not cover the Channel Islands. Every value on the grid is an estimate for the centre point of a 1km by 1km grid box, the most detailed climate data publicly available for the UK. The values are created using observations from land-based weather stations across the country, and by taking into account additional factors such as altitude, terrain and distance from the coast to scientifically “fill in the gaps” between weather stations. 
The results displayed for each grid area represents a mean average of that grid cell and its nearest grid cells. For most areas, this represents a 5km square centred on the primary grid cell. Along irregular coastlines and on small islands, the nearest grid cells are chosen to match the shape of the coastline or island, but no cells are further than 7km away.

A rare wildflower may have been wiped out in southern England after a summer of record heat and drought, conservationists have warned.




The field gentian, once widespread across Britain, was until recently so abundant in the New Forest in Hampshire that conservationists said counting the flowers was a challenge.








But after 2026 brought record warmth, successive heatwaves and severe drought — the third extreme summer in just five years — the plant may have disappeared from southern England altogether.




Experts described its possible disappearance as a “canary in the mine” for climate-driven species loss.




The Species Recovery Trust, a charity working to save some of Britain’s most endangered species, said the potential loss was “deeply worrying” because the field gentian had previously been abundant wherever it grew.


Dry and barren land in southern England following the summer's record-breaking heatwaves
The Species Recovery Trust/PA Wire




Dominic Price, director of the Species Recovery Trust, said the plant’s habitat — dry, “skeletal” grassland — was on the “absolute front line” of climate change.













“These habitats are becoming parched and dead in hot, dry weather,” he said.




The field gentian’s disappearance would be a striking example of how increasingly frequent heat and drought can push even locally abundant species towards extinction.




In 2022, when temperatures in the UK soared to 40C for the first time on record amid an extremely hot, dry summer, field gentian populations crashed for the first time across all known sites in the south of England, and went extinct at a county-level in Devon.









Populations recovered slightly the following year, and it was thought the New Forest populations could survive, due to their sheer size – often more than 5,000 plants at each site – and their ability for seeds to move with livestock into more sheltered areas.




But then populations were hit by successive record hot summers and droughts, in 2025 and again this year.


Field gentians growing in southern England

The Species Recovery Trust has confirmed it has been unable to locate a single field gentian plant in the New Forest for the second year in a row.

Hundreds of thousands are expected to die, millions to go hungry. This is not just about weather patterns, but about injustice





Some warnings are so grave that it is almost impossible to fully comprehend them. They say that the weather pattern, which occurs roughly every two to seven years, may be the strongest in at least a millennium. Interview
Gavin Newsom condemns Democrats’ ‘climate hushing’, predicts Trump’s downfall and expects AOC to run in 2028

Mark Hertsgaard


Democrats must show links of climate shocks to ‘kitchen table’ issues, California governor says




It’s a mistake for Democratic politicians not to talk about climate change, and the reason they don’t is “because they don’t know how to talk about it”, the California governor, Gavin Newsom, said on Wednesday in an interview with the Guardian and the global journalism collaboration Covering Climate Now.
Speaking on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly meeting and New York Climate Week, Newsom also predicted that the midterm elections in November would bring “the end of Donald Trump’s presidency as we know it”. To prevent Trump from stealing those elections, voters must turn out in such overwhelming numbers that he “couldn’t possibly contest” the outcome. If the US president nevertheless declares a national emergency or otherwise attempts to invalidate the results, Newsom said, then “we the people have to step up. The courts have to intervene. Congress has to do its job and stand up for the rule of law.”



Although Newsom said in an interview with CNN last week that he would not run for president if Kamala Harris did, on Wednesday he did not rule out running if US representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez decides to run.
Commenting on Covering Climate Now and the Guardian reporting that 80% to 89% of the world’s people and 74% of Americans want their governments to take stronger climate action, Newsom condemned the “climate hushing” most Democrats have practiced since Trump returned to the White House in 2025. “I talk about [climate change] all the time,” he said. He agreed that Democrats must be “laser-focused” on voters’ affordability concerns, but the key is to “connect the dots” between those concerns and the economic impacts of extreme heat, droughts, floods, and other consequences of overheating the planet.
